metadata.title: Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. v. FCC, 520 U.S. 180 (1997) (No. 95-992)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. v. FCC

Opinion filed: 1997-03-31

Docket No.: 95-992

Citations:
• 137 L. Ed. 2d 369
• 117 S. Ct. 1174
• 520 U.S. 180
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 2078

Case holding summaries:
• finding consumer protection to be a legitimate governmental interest
• controlling opinion of Kennedy, J.
• content-neutral regulation of speech warrants only intermediate scrutiny protection
• “[I]n the realm of First Amendment questions,” the legislature “must base its conclusions upon substantial evidence.”
• "A content-neutral regulation will be sustained under the First Amendment if it advances important governmental interests unrelated to the suppression of free speech and does not burden substantially more speech than necessary to further those interests." (emphasis added)
• applying the aforementioned O'Brien test to content-neutral restrictions on public broadcasting
• noting that the congressional record included "years of testimony and reviewing volumes of documentary evidence and studies offered by both sides" compiled three years of hearings
• finding consumer protec- tion to be a legitimate federal governmental interest
• "Congress is not obligated, when enacting its statutes, to make a record of the type that an administrative agency or court does to accommodate judicial review."
• coerced carriage of broadcast signals over cable television facilities
• holding that "Congress has drawn reasonable inferences based on substantial evidence," when it had before it evidence including some memory surveys
• "We do not believe. . . [that] United States v. O'Brien . . . endow[s] the judiciary with the competence to judge how much protection of park lands is wise"
• overnight camping ban upheld although "there [were] less speech-restrictive alternatives" of satisfying interest in preserving park lands
• "None of [the regulation's] provisions appears unrelated to the ends that it was designed to serve"
• separate opinion of Stevens, J.
• it was "beyond the competence of the Court of Appeals itself to assess the relative risks and benefits" of FCC policy, so long as that policy was based on findings supported by evidence
• scope of law must be "in proportion to the interest served"
• statement of Edward O. Fritts
• time, place, and manner restriction
• holding regulation valid although Court of Appeals had identified less restrictive "alternative regulatory methods" of controlling volume at concerts
• "[T]he essence of narrow tailoring" is "focus[ing] on the source of the evils the [Government] seeks to eliminate [without] significantly restricting a substantial quantity of speech that does not create the same evils"
• "`This Court has recognized the strong governmental interest in certain forms of economic regulation, even though such regulation may have an incidental effect on rights of speech and association' " (quoting NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co., 458 U. S. 886, 912 (1982))
• referring to studies "showing the dominant role of television stations. . . as sources of local news and other information"
• "`While many of the network practices raise serious questions under the antitrust laws, . . . [i]t is not [the FCC's] function to apply the antitrust laws as such' " (quoting FCC Report on Chain Broadcasting Regulations (1941))
• mandatory over-the-air broadcasts to be carried by cable networks raises serious freedom of speech issues
• describing interest in ensuring that broadcast television remains available as a source of video programming for those without cable
• describing interest in "protecting noncable households from loss of regular television broadcasting service" (emphasis added; internal quotation marks omitted)
• stating that although making exceptions to ban on posting signs on public property "would have had a less severe effect on expressive activity," they were not "constitutionally mandated"
• courts must perform "appropriately deferential examination of Congress' evaluation of th[e] evidence"
• upholding validity of order barring a person from a military base, although excluding barred person was not "essential" to preserving security and there were less speech-restrictive means of attaining that end
• discussing deference due to Congress's findings
• “In reviewing the constitutionality of a statute, ‘courts must accord substantial deference to the predictive judgments of Congress.’”
• holding that in reviewing content-neutral regulations burdening speech under an intermediate scrutiny standard, the question for the courts "is whether the legislative conclusion was reasonable and supported bysubstantial evidence in the record before [the legislative body]"
• requiring “ad vance[ment of] important governmental interests unre lated to the suppression of free speech” without “bur den[ing] substantially more speech than necessary to further those interests”
• declining to decide question that received only “scant argumentation”
• finding consumer protection a legitimate federal governmental interest in a First Amendment challenge
• "Congress is not obligated, when enacting its statutes, to make a record of the type that an administrative agency or court does to accommodate judicial review."
• "In reviewing the constitutionality of a statute, "courts must accord substantial deference to the predictive judgments of Congress.' "
• “promoting the widespread dissemination of information from a multiplicity of sources” is an important government interest
• if the determination is reasonable and supported by substantial evidence on the record, summary judgment is appropriate Consolidated Court No. 06-00173 Page 20 regardless of whether the evidence is in conflict
• requiring courts to "accord substantial deference to the predictive judgments of Congress" in First Amendment cases
